paragraphs: This paper examines a tension in neural network architecture: abundant connections support interactions among representations, but they may also interfere with carrying out independent tasks simultaneously. The authors turn this question into a graph problem, representing tasks as edges between two groups of resources. This makes the relationship between connectivity and multitasking capacity mathematically explicit.

The analysis rests on two stated assumptions. Tasks that need to run together use independent resources, represented by a matching: a collection of edges without shared endpoints. An induced matching supplies the condition under which tasks can run without interference. The authors use these ideas to define a measure of multitasking capacity.

Their main result establishes a tradeoff between this capacity and average connectivity, regardless of architecture within the framework. They extend the results to deeper networks and identify favorable multitasking properties in random-like, locally sparse networks. The contribution is a structural explanation of parallel-processing limits under the stated task and interference assumptions.
neurips-2017-a-graph-theoretic-approach-.tldr: A graph-based model establishes a tradeoff between network connectivity and interference-free multitasking under explicit resource assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper develops a new alternating-direction approach to linear programming. Its starting point is a practical weakness of an established method: although convergence is globally linear, progress near the solution can become slow and fluctuate. Its stated convergence bound also includes explicit dependence on the dimensions of the constraint matrix.

The authors change how the linear program's variables are split into parts for optimization. They prove a convergence rate of O(||A||² log(1/ε)), compared with the cited O((||A||F² + mn) log(1/ε)) rate. The proof jointly relates residuals to the distances of primal and dual iterates from their respective optimal solution sets. This supplies a way to assess progress on both sides of the optimization problem.

The resulting first-order solver can exploit sparsity and specific structure in the constraint matrix. The authors report significant speedups over leading linear-programming solvers on problems including basis pursuit, inverse covariance estimation, L1 support vector machines, and nonnegative matrix factorization. These practical findings accompany the improved theoretical rate.
neurips-2017-a-new-alternating-direction.tldr: A new variable-splitting method improves a linear-programming convergence bound and delivers reported speedups on several applications.

paragraphs: Batch normalization can make deep models train faster and more effectively, but its benefits weaken when training batches are small or contain dependent examples. This paper investigates an extension aimed at those conditions. The authors hypothesize that the difficulty comes from two related features: a layer's inputs depend on other examples in the batch, and activations differ between training and inference.

Batch Renormalization is designed to align the outputs produced during training and inference while making them depend on individual examples rather than the entire minibatch. The key idea is to change the normalization behavior so that the surrounding batch has less influence on how an example is processed. This directly addresses the mechanism proposed in the authors' hypothesis.

The reported models substantially outperform batch normalization when trained with small or non-independent minibatches. They also retain training efficiency and reduced sensitivity to initialization. These findings support the extension's usefulness under the batch conditions studied, while the explanation of why ordinary batch normalization struggles remains explicitly framed as a hypothesis.
neurips-2017-batch-renormalization-towar.tldr: Batch Renormalization improves training with small or dependent minibatches by aligning training and inference behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies how discrete and continuous methods relate when minimizing decomposable submodular functions. Both families address the same optimization problem, but their connection is the central subject of the work. The authors examine that connection through theoretical running-time analysis and a systematic comparison of algorithm behavior in experiments.

The theoretical contribution uses combinatorial arguments to obtain improved running-time estimates for leading continuous algorithms. This matters because it shows that reasoning associated with discrete structure can sharpen our understanding of continuous approaches. The stated improvement concerns the estimates for these algorithms, so the contribution is a better analysis of their computational requirements rather than an asserted new solver.

The experimental contribution compares the two families while explicitly distinguishing level-0 from level-1 algorithms. That distinction provides an organizing basis for the comparison, alongside the theoretical connection. Together, the contributions make the relationship between discrete and continuous methods more concrete: discrete arguments improve continuous-method analysis, and experiments systematically examine the alternatives within a shared classification.
neurips-2017-decomposable-submodular-fun.tldr: Combinatorial analysis sharpens running-time estimates for continuous submodular minimization methods, alongside a systematic comparison with discrete approaches.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way for a single neural text-to-speech system to produce many different voices. Each speaker receives a small, trainable numerical representation, called an embedding. The embedding provides speaker-specific information within a shared model, allowing the system to learn different voices without requiring a separate full model for each person.

The authors first improve two single-speaker systems. Deep Voice 2 follows a pipeline similar to Deep Voice 1 but uses stronger components, producing a significant reported improvement in audio quality. They also improve Tacotron by adding a neural vocoder as a post-processing stage. These changes provide stronger speech-generation systems to which the speaker-embedding technique can be applied.

The multi-speaker approach is demonstrated with both systems on two datasets. The authors report that one model can learn hundreds of voices using less than half an hour of data per speaker, while maintaining high audio quality and almost perfectly preserving speaker identities. The results support sharing a synthesis model while retaining distinct speaker characteristics.
neurips-2017-deep-voice-2-multi-speaker-.tldr: Trainable speaker embeddings let one improved text-to-speech model synthesize hundreds of distinct voices from limited data per speaker.

paragraphs: Conventional encoder-decoder systems generate an output sequence in a single forward pass and then treat it as finished. This paper adds a revision stage, motivated by the way people polish written material. Its deliberation network separates producing an initial sequence from refining that sequence into the final output.

The architecture contains two levels of decoders. The first produces a draft, and the second uses that draft while generating a refined version. Because the draft already contains later words, the second decoder has access to global information about a possible complete sentence. That gives it the potential to make better decisions than a decoder working only through its first attempt.

Experiments in machine translation and text summarization demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. On WMT 2014 English-to-French translation, the authors report a BLEU score of 41.5, which they identify as a new state of the art. The findings support draft-based refinement as a useful sequence-generation strategy; the architectural benefit is access to future draft content, not a guarantee that every revision improves every sentence.
neurips-2017-deliberation-networks-seque.tldr: Deliberation networks generate a draft and then refine it with a second decoder that can inspect the whole draft.

paragraphs: Crowding occurs when nearby objects make a target difficult to recognize even though it is recognizable alone. This paper tests that effect in deep neural networks. It compares standard convolutional networks with eccentricity-dependent networks, whose filter receptive fields vary with image position and operate at multiple scales.

When trained on isolated targets, the eccentricity-dependent model can recognize targets surrounded by flankers near the image center, whereas the tested standard convolutional networks cannot. Across all tested networks trained on isolated targets, recognition declines as flankers move closer or become more numerous. Similarity between targets and flankers also affects recognition, and pooling in early layers increases crowding.

The authors additionally train networks on images containing flankers. This does not produce robustness to configurations absent from training. The findings show that architecture, target position, and the arrangement of surrounding objects all matter in the tested settings. They also establish a specific generalization limit: exposure to some crowded scenes does not ensure resistance to unfamiliar crowding configurations.
neurips-2017-do-deep-neural-networks-suf.tldr: Tested recognition networks exhibit crowding, with sensitivity shaped by architecture, flanker arrangement, and training configurations.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, the current observation may not contain enough information for predicting what happens next. Models can therefore need histories of observations, but existing variable-order approaches have substantial memory requirements and can confuse histories because of sensor noise. This paper introduces dynamic-depth context tree weighting, or D2-CTW, to address these difficulties.

D2-CTW grows a suffix tree dynamically while bounding the total model size rather than its depth. The distinction matters: limiting memory usage does not require imposing a fixed maximum history length. The model can represent long histories while remaining within a bounded overall size, adapting its representation as learning proceeds.

For stochastic time-series prediction, the method approximately matches leading alternatives while using at least ten times less memory. In model-based reinforcement learning tasks requiring past observations, it can learn without advance knowledge of a suitable state representation or the necessary history length. These results demonstrate useful memory efficiency and adaptive history modeling in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2017-dynamic-depth-context-tree-.tldr: D2-CTW learns variable-length observation histories with bounded model size, achieving competitive prediction with substantially less memory.

paragraphs: This paper asks how well image representations explain which small image changes humans can notice. It develops a comparison method based on Fisher information, which translates a model's representation into predictions of sensitivity to local image perturbations. The method links a mathematical property of the representation to a directly measured perceptual response.

For each image, the authors find directions associated with the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the Fisher information matrix. These correspond to distortions the model predicts should be most and least noticeable. Human participants then view these distortions, and the authors measure how much distortion is needed for reliable detection.

Early VGG16 layers match human sensitivity better than later layers and better than a four-stage network trained on image-quality ratings. However, simple early-vision models incorporating local gain control, trained on the same ratings, predict sensitivity substantially better than either that network or any combination of VGG16 layers. The findings distinguish success at object recognition or quality-rating prediction from success at explaining the tested human detection thresholds.
neurips-2017-eigen-distortions-of-hierar.tldr: Model-derived image distortions reveal that simple gain-control models predict tested human visual sensitivity better than the evaluated deep representations.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings can contain patterns of activity that evolve along a much smaller set of underlying dimensions. This paper develops a method for recovering those dynamics from multiple sequential recordings. The motivation is that methods restricted to a single recording cannot identify dynamics distributed across separate measurements of a larger neural population.

The method builds on subspace identification for dynamical systems. It estimates parameters by matching moments, training the model to predict how neural activity covaries across neurons and over time. A scalable stochastic gradient descent procedure minimizes this objective. This approach connects separate observations through their temporal statistical relationships.

The algorithm scales to millions of observed dimensions and naturally accommodates missing data and partial recordings. The authors show that it can identify dynamics and predict correlations despite severe subsampling and little overlap between recordings. Demonstrations use simulated data and whole-brain imaging of larval zebrafish. The contribution expands the range of recordings that can be combined to study shared low-dimensional neural dynamics.
neurips-2017-extracting-low-dimensional-.tldr: Matching temporal correlations allows scalable recovery of low-dimensional neural dynamics across multiple incomplete recordings.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from measurements that retain magnitudes but lose phase information. Because this problem is ill-posed, recovery requires additional assumptions about the signal or measurements. This paper focuses on sparse signals, where only s of n entries are nonzero, and on signals whose nonzero entries occur in blocks.

The proposed CoPRAM algorithm combines alternating minimization for phase retrieval with CoSaMP for sparse recovery. With Gaussian measurements, the authors prove a sample complexity of O(s² log n), matching the best existing results cited in the abstract. They also establish linear convergence, observe it in practice, and require no additional tuning parameter beyond the sparsity level.

Block CoPRAM uses uniform block structure to reduce the measurement requirement to O(ks log n), where k is the number of active blocks. When block length is proportional to s, this becomes O(s log n). Thus, stronger structural information can improve sample requirements. The authors qualify their novelty claim as the first known end-to-end linearly convergent family achieving subquadratic sparsity dependence under Gaussian measurements.
neurips-2017-fast-sample-efficient-algor.tldr: CoPRAM combines sparse recovery and alternating minimization, with block structure enabling lower Gaussian measurement requirements.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a neural architecture for recognizing text in natural images. It builds on recurrent convolutional networks, which combine image processing with recurrent information. The proposed Gated RCNN adds a mechanism for controlling how that recurrent context interacts with information arriving through the feed-forward path.

Its central component is the gated recurrent convolution layer. A gate regulates context modulation and balances feed-forward information against recurrent information. This makes the balance between the two information sources an explicit part of the architecture. The authors also construct an efficient bidirectional long short-term memory network to model sequences, combining it with the gated convolutional network.

The complete GRCNN-BLSTM system can be trained end to end, bringing the image-processing and sequence-modeling components into one trainable recognition model. Experiments report better performance than existing methods on several text-recognition benchmarks, including IIIT-5K, Street View Text, and ICDAR. These results support the combined architecture for the evaluated natural-image text tasks, with gating providing its distinctive way of regulating contextual information.
neurips-2017-gated-recurrent-convolution.tldr: A gated recurrent convolutional network combined with bidirectional sequence modeling improves text recognition on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Spectral methods of moments learn the parameters of latent-variable models from statistical summaries of observed data. Although these methods have appealing theoretical properties, the paper identifies a practical obstacle: they can lack robustness when the assumed model does not match the data. That mismatch limits how readily their theoretical appeal translates into useful results on real datasets.

The authors propose a hierarchical approach to methods of moments. Its central computational change replaces the tensor-decomposition step used by earlier algorithms with approximate joint diagonalization. This changes a key operation in parameter learning while retaining the broader methods-of-moments approach. The replacement is presented as a way to address difficulties associated with model misspecification.

Experiments in topic modeling show improvements over previous tensor-decomposition methods in both speed and model quality. These two findings matter together: the alternative computation is faster in the reported tests and also produces better models. The evidence supports the hierarchical approach for the evaluated topic-modeling setting, without making robustness to every possible model mismatch a universal guarantee.
neurips-2017-hierarchical-methods-of-mom.tldr: Replacing tensor decomposition with approximate joint diagonalization improves reported topic-modeling speed and quality.

paragraphs: Many image-processing tasks benefit from knowing which image locations should be treated as similar. This paper learns those relationships through a spatial propagation network. Instead of constructing similarity kernels from the features of two points, the approach learns task-specific affinities directly from data, including relationships informed by semantic content.

The network propagates information linearly along rows or columns. A three-way connection structure gives it a sparse transformation matrix whose entries can be produced by a deep convolutional network. Despite that sparse underlying transformation, propagation yields a dense affinity matrix representing global pairwise relationships. The distinction matters because a compact propagation structure can describe relationships throughout an image.

The authors present the framework as applicable to tasks such as matting, colorization, and guided filtering, and validate it through object-segmentation refinement. Experiments on HELEN face parsing and PASCAL VOC-2012 semantic segmentation support its effectiveness and efficiency in producing high-quality segmentations. These demonstrations show how learned affinities can refine segmentation, while the other named uses describe the framework's broader applicability.
neurips-2017-learning-affinity-via-spati.tldr: Spatial propagation turns learned sparse transformations into dense image affinities that effectively refine segmentation.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to reduce a trained neural network's size while preserving prediction performance. The motivation is especially relevant to embedded applications, where compact models are valuable. The authors identify a tension in existing pruning approaches: some achieve limited compression, while others need substantial retraining to recover performance after removing parameters.

Their method prunes each layer independently using second-order derivatives of a layer-specific error function. These derivatives guide parameter removal through the behavior of that layer's error. The authors also prove that the final prediction-performance drop is bounded by a linear combination of the reconstruction errors introduced at individual layers.

That bound connects local pruning decisions to the behavior of the entire network. With layer errors controlled appropriately, the authors state that light retraining suffices to restore original prediction performance. This is a conditional claim tied to error control. Extensive benchmark experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness against several leading pruning approaches, supporting its practical use alongside the theoretical connection between layer errors and final performance.
neurips-2017-learning-to-prune-deep-neur.tldr: Layer-wise second-order pruning links local reconstruction errors to overall performance loss, enabling light retraining when errors are controlled.

paragraphs: Ordinary regression assumes that each input is paired with its corresponding response. This paper considers the harder setting where those pairings are unknown. It studies both how to compute a fitted linear function and what statistical conditions permit recovery, separating algorithmic possibilities from information limits.

First, the authors give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the natural least-squares problem when dimension is fixed. This provides an efficient route to increasingly accurate optimization in any constant dimension. A second result handles arbitrary dimension, but under stronger assumptions: inputs are independent standard Gaussian draws, responses are noiseless, and an exact linear relationship generates them.

In that average-case, noise-free setting, an efficient algorithm using lattice basis reduction exactly recovers the unknown linear function. The paper also establishes lower bounds on the signal-to-noise ratio required for approximate recovery by any estimator. Together, the results distinguish what can be optimized efficiently in fixed dimension, what can be recovered exactly under a specific data model, and what noise fundamentally prevents.
neurips-2017-linear-regression-without-c.tldr: Regression with unknown input-response pairings admits efficient algorithms under stated conditions and fundamental signal-to-noise limits.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an efficiently optimizable function remains easy to minimize when it is available only through training examples. The setting is submodular minimization. Although submodular functions can be minimized efficiently when the function is available, practical learning problems may provide only samples from which to learn it.

The authors construct a class of functions taking values between zero and one that are both PAC-learnable and minimizable in polynomial time. Nevertheless, polynomially many samples do not permit an algorithm to achieve an approximation strictly better than the stated 1/2 − o(1) threshold. The result applies to samples drawn from any distribution and establishes a barrier for every algorithm in this sample-access setting.

A trivial algorithm attains an approximation of 1/2, making the bound tight in the sense described by the paper. The central lesson is that learning and optimization can have different information requirements. A function class may support successful learning and efficient direct minimization, yet its sampled values may still be insufficient for obtaining a better minimizing solution.
neurips-2017-minimizing-a-submodular-fun.tldr: Some efficiently learnable and minimizable submodular functions cannot be minimized beyond a tight approximation threshold from polynomially many samples.

paragraphs: This paper revisits maximum-likelihood estimation for linear dynamical systems with generalized-linear observation models. The difficulty is that hidden states and the parameters governing their transitions must be inferred together. The authors describe expectation-maximization as difficult to scale and susceptible to local minima, while commonly used moment-matching alternatives have statistical-efficiency issues.

Their strategy reformulates maximum-likelihood estimation into a two-view problem. This makes global optimization algorithms for matrix factorization available for recovering both latent states and transition parameters. The contribution is therefore a different optimization formulation of the likelihood problem, opening a route that avoids abandoning likelihood estimation in favor of moment matching.

The authors report better accuracy and runtime than widely used system-identification algorithms, including subspace-identification methods. Those results support reconsidering likelihood-based estimation in this setting: a problem regarded as difficult can become more practical through its mathematical representation. The reported comparison concerns the proposed strategy and the evaluated identification methods, while the two-view formulation supplies the mechanism that enables the new approach.
neurips-2017-multi-view-matrix-factoriza.tldr: A two-view matrix-factorization formulation makes likelihood-based dynamical-system estimation more accurate and faster in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper studies least-squares regression when the unknown parameter is a low-rank tensor, a multidimensional array represented through smaller components. Such a representation can require far fewer parameters than treating every array entry independently. The authors consider both CP and Tucker decompositions and ask how this structure can also reduce the size of the regression computation.

Their approach applies a sparse random projection to both the model predictions and the observed response vector. This produces a smaller least-squares problem. The theoretical guarantee preserves squared residuals within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± ε simultaneously for every tensor in the considered model class, so preservation is not restricted to a single chosen candidate.

By exploiting low-rank tensor structure, the authors obtain smaller projection dimensions and greater sparsity than are possible for ordinary least-squares regression. Numerical simulations support the theory. The contribution connects compact parameter structure with compact data processing: the regression problem can be reduced while retaining a uniform approximation to its objective across candidate tensors.
neurips-2017-near-optimal-sketching-of-l.tldr: Sparse random projections shrink low-rank tensor regression while uniformly preserving its least-squares objective approximately.

paragraphs: This paper develops kernels for Gaussian process regression when relationships between inputs change across the input space. Its target is non-stationary data, where one uniform pattern of dependence is inadequate. The proposed kernels can also express non-monotonic relationships, allowing covariance to vary in ways that are not simply a steady decline with separation.

The authors model spectral density using a mixture of input-dependent frequency-density surfaces governed by Gaussian processes. They solve the generalized Fourier transform for this construction to obtain a family of kernels. The resulting covariance functions can learn relationships that depend on location and may extend over long distances while remaining non-monotonic.

The paper also derives efficient inference through model whitening and a marginalized posterior. Case studies cover time series, images, and geospatial data with non-stationary characteristics. In those examples, the authors show the need for these kernels even with relatively simple data. The findings motivate richer covariance models for the demonstrated patterns, rather than establishing that every dataset requires non-stationary modeling.
neurips-2017-non-stationary-spectral-ker.tldr: Input-dependent spectral models yield Gaussian process kernels that capture changing, potentially long-range and non-monotonic relationships.

paragraphs: This paper studies planning for populations of agents whose collective behavior affects both shared rewards and how the environment evolves. It focuses on CDec-POMDPs, a particular subclass of decentralized partially observable decision problems. The narrower setting is motivated by the computational difficulty of solving general decentralized multiagent problems.

The authors develop an actor-critic reinforcement-learning method for optimizing policies in this setting. Standard actor-critic learning converges slowly on larger problems, so they change how the approximate action-value function is represented. A particular decomposition across agents leads to more effective policy updates. They also derive a new procedure for training the critic from local reward signals.

These changes connect population-level planning with learning signals organized around individual agents. Comparisons on a synthetic benchmark and a real-world taxi fleet optimization problem produce higher-quality solutions than previous leading approaches. The findings support this decomposition and critic-training strategy for collective multiagent planning, with the problem structure providing the basis for the method rather than an unrestricted solution to every decentralized planning problem.
neurips-2017-policy-gradient-with-value-.tldr: An agent-wise value decomposition and locally trained critic improve reported solutions for collective multiagent planning.

paragraphs: Motivated by online advertising, this paper studies sequential choices involving several display slots. Later slots produce fewer rewards, but the extent of this position bias is unknown. Learning must therefore account for both the options being selected and the effects of their positions, rather than attributing observed rewards entirely to the selected options.

The authors characterize the problem's difficulty through an asymptotic regret bound. Regret measures reward lost through learning and imperfect decisions. They propose the Permutation Minimum Empirical Divergence algorithm, or PMED, and derive an asymptotically optimal regret bound for it. This establishes optimality in the long-run sense specified by the analysis.

Unknown position bias creates non-convex optimization problems within the optimal algorithm, differing from those in usual partial-monitoring and semi-bandit settings. To handle these computations, the paper proposes a cutting-plane method and a related bi-convex relaxation using auxiliary variables. Its contributions therefore address both the statistical difficulty of learning with unknown position effects and the optimization work required by the proposed algorithm.
neurips-2017-position-based-multiple-pla.tldr: PMED achieves asymptotically optimal regret for multi-slot bandits with unknown position bias, alongside methods for its non-convex computations.

paragraphs: This paper develops first-order stochastic approximation algorithms for canonical correlation analysis, or CCA. Its focus is on obtaining useful optimization guarantees for stochastic procedures. The authors evaluate progress against the population objective, so the target of the guarantee is the underlying statistical objective rather than only an objective computed from a particular finite dataset.

The proposed algorithms are inexact versions of matrix stochastic gradient and matrix exponentiated gradient methods. The analysis shows that they achieve ε-suboptimality in a number of iterations polynomial in 1/ε. In plain language, the objective can be brought within a chosen tolerance of optimality with an iteration requirement that grows polynomially as that tolerance becomes stricter.

The paper also considers practical variants and compares its methods with other CCA approaches both theoretically and empirically. This combines convergence analysis with an examination of implementations intended for use. The stated contribution is a family of stochastic algorithms with population-level accuracy guarantees and comparative evaluation; the abstract does not claim that one method dominates all alternatives.
neurips-2017-stochastic-approximation-fo.tldr: Inexact stochastic matrix-gradient methods for CCA achieve population-objective accuracy in polynomially many iterations.

paragraphs: This paper brings stochastic continuous optimization to discrete submodular maximization. It considers objectives defined as expectations, which can arise either from empirical data or from an explicit random model. The abstract gives exemplar-based clustering and social-network influence maximization as examples of these two sources of stochastic objectives.

The approach moves the problem into a continuous domain, uses projected stochastic gradient ascent or related methods, and then rounds the result into a discrete solution. A key mathematical ingredient is that common extensions act linearly on submodular functions. The authors focus their guarantees on weighted coverage functions, a rich family within the broader submodular setting.

For that family, the method matches optimal approximation guarantees. This means it preserves the stated quality guarantee for an approximate solution, rather than claiming exact optimization. Experiments demonstrate computational-cost reductions of several orders of magnitude. The theoretical and empirical contributions complement each other: approximation quality is guaranteed, while the magnitude of the computational savings is established through the reported experiments.
neurips-2017-stochastic-submodular-maxim.tldr: Continuous stochastic optimization and rounding achieve optimal approximation guarantees for weighted coverage objectives with large empirical computational savings.

paragraphs: Structured Generative Adversarial Networks address conditional generation with limited labeled supervision. The goal is to control designated semantics in generated samples while separating those semantics from other variation. The model assumes two independent latent variables: y represents the designated meaning or structure, and z represents the remaining factors.

SGAN uses two collaborative games that minimize reconstruction errors for y and z, encouraging the intended separation. It also trains through two adversarial games whose equilibria concentrate on the true joint distributions of data with each latent variable. This ties both semantic and other latent information to the observed data while addressing diffuse probability allocation that maximum-likelihood methods may exhibit.

The authors report controllable generation and disentangled representations, as well as state-of-the-art semi-supervised classification results across three datasets. Reported errors are 1.27% on MNIST with 50 labels, 5.73% on SVHN with 1,000, and 17.26% on CIFAR-10 with 4,000. They also report high-quality images that follow designated semantics and describe extensions such as style transfer.
neurips-2017-structured-generative-adver.tldr: SGAN separates semantic and other latent factors to support controllable image generation and strong semi-supervised classification.
